title: Search and Replace After Domain Change
description: Site files are on the new domain. The database still contains the old domain in every option, URL, and serialized value. Replace it safely.
instructions: You are SSH'd into /var/www/html on the new server. The site is reachable but internal links and images point to the old domain. Execute steps in order.

steps.feedback_wrong: Before replacing anything, read the current state. Confirm the old domain is still in the database.
steps.feedback_correct: Confirmed — the database still uses the old domain. Export before changing anything.

steps.feedback_wrong: Always export the database before a search-replace. If the replacement goes wrong, this file restores the old state.
steps.feedback_correct: Backup in place. Now preview the scope before committing.

steps.hint: Preview how many rows will change — without writing anything to the database
steps.feedback_wrong: Use --dry-run to preview the scope before committing. Never run search-replace on production without checking the count first.
steps.feedback_correct: 1100 rows will change — that matches a typical site. Now run the actual replacement.

steps.feedback_wrong: The dry run confirmed the scope. Remove --dry-run and run the actual replacement.
steps.feedback_correct: 1100 replacements made. Verify the siteurl now shows the new domain.

content.goal: Replace all occurrences of an old domain with a new domain across every WordPress database table — options, posts, postmeta, and serialized data — without breaking the site and with a full rollback point in place.

steps.title: 1. Check the current siteurl
paragraphs: Before changing anything, read the current state. The siteurl and home options are the canonical domain reference in WordPress — if they still show the old domain, the database has not been updated.
This step confirms you are targeting the right domain and connected to the right database. Running search-replace against the wrong database is an unrecoverable mistake without a backup.

steps.title: 2. Export the database
paragraphs: A search-replace touches thousands of rows across multiple tables and modifies serialized PHP data. If the replacement produces unexpected results — wrong row count, encoding issue, wrong domain pattern — you need to be able to restore instantly.
Export to a timestamped filename. On production, move the dump off-server to a backup destination immediately after export — a backup on the same disk is not a real backup.

steps.title: 3. Dry run — preview the scope
paragraphs: The --dry-run flag shows exactly how many rows in which tables will be changed, without writing anything to the database. On production this is not optional — run it every time.
Check the Changed column. If wp_options shows 0 changes, the domain pattern is likely wrong. If the count is unexpectedly high, double-check the search string before proceeding.

steps.title: 4. Run the replacement
paragraphs: WP-CLI handles PHP serialized data correctly — it updates the string length in the serialized wrapper alongside the value itself. Manual SQL UPDATE statements break serialization; wp search-replace does not.
Use --all-tables to reach custom plugin tables, WooCommerce tables, and any table outside the standard WordPress prefix. Without this flag, those tables keep the old domain.

steps.title: 5. Verify the siteurl
paragraphs: Read the siteurl option after the replacement. It should now return the new domain. This is the fastest single-field confirmation that the core option was updated correctly.
Also check wp option get home — WordPress uses both siteurl (where WordPress is installed) and home (the public-facing URL). Both must point to the new domain.

steps.title: 6. Flush cache and rewrite rules
paragraphs: The object cache may hold stale values from before the replacement — cached option values, transients, or fragment caches with old domain strings. Flushing forces a fresh read from the updated database.
Rewrite rules are stored in the database and cached in memory. After a domain change, WordPress must rebuild them against the new home URL so all permalink structures resolve correctly.
steps.command: wp cache flush && wp rewrite flush

troubleshooting: Running wp search-replace without --dry-run first on production — you have no preview of the scope and no way to catch a wrong domain pattern before it's applied to thousands of rows.
Not using --all-tables — custom plugin tables, WooCommerce tables, and third-party data keep the old domain even after all standard tables are updated.

Replacing only the naked domain but missing the protocol — if the database contains both http:// and https:// variants of the old domain, run two passes or replace the naked domain without protocol to cover both.
Skipping wp db export before the replacement — if serialized data breaks or the wrong pattern is applied, there is no clean restore point.
Not flushing cache after the replacement — the object cache returns stale old-domain values for minutes or hours after the database is updated.

Forgetting to check if WP_HOME or WP_SITEURL constants are defined in wp-config.php — those constants override the database options and will keep serving the old domain regardless of what search-replace did.

faq.question: Why use --all-tables instead of the default scope?
faq.answer: By default, wp search-replace only searches tables with the WordPress table prefix (wp_posts, wp_options, etc.). WooCommerce, BuddyPress, and many other plugins create tables under different names. --all-tables searches every table in the database, including those outside the standard prefix.

faq.question: Does wp search-replace handle serialized PHP data correctly?
faq.answer: Yes. WP-CLI recalculates the byte-length in the serialized string wrapper after replacing the value. Manual SQL UPDATE statements break serialization because the stored length no longer matches the actual string — WordPress throws unserialization errors on every request. Always use WP-CLI for domain replacements, never raw SQL.

faq.question: Should I replace the protocol (http/https) or just the domain?
faq.answer: If you are also changing protocol, replace the full URL. Run two passes: first wp search-replace 'http://oldsite.com' 'https://newsite.com' --all-tables, then wp search-replace 'https://oldsite.com' 'https://newsite.com' --all-tables. If the protocol stays the same, replacing the naked domain (without protocol) covers both variants in a single pass.

faq.question: What if the row count in --dry-run is much higher than expected?
faq.answer: Stop before running without --dry-run. A high count may mean your search string appears as a substring inside other unrelated values. Use --include-columns=guid,option_value,post_content to restrict which columns are searched, or narrow the pattern to include the protocol.

faq.question: Can I roll back the search-replace if something goes wrong?
faq.answer: Yes — if you exported the database in step 2, restore with wp db import backup-before-replace.sql. This returns all tables to the pre-replacement state. This is the only reason the export step is never optional.

faq.question: Do I need to update wp-config.php after a domain change?
faq.answer: Only if WP_HOME or WP_SITEURL constants are defined in wp-config.php — those constants override whatever is in the database. If they are set and still point to the old domain, search-replace alone will not fix the site. Update the constants in wp-config.php first, then run search-replace.

seo.title: Search and Replace Domain with WP-CLI — Practice Case
seo.description: Practice replacing a domain across all WordPress database tables after migration: dry run, search-replace with --all-tables, verify siteurl, flush cache. Interactive WP-CLI terminal.

perfect: You ran --dry-run before the actual replacement — the habit that catches wrong domain patterns before they propagate across thousands of rows.
You exported the database before touching it — a full restore point available throughout the entire process.
optimize: Run wp search-replace with --report-changed-only to get cleaner output showing only tables that actually changed.
After the replacement, run wp option list --search='*oldsite*' to catch any options the search-replace did not reach.
Move the database backup off the server immediately after export — S3, remote storage, or any off-disk destination.
If WP_HOME or WP_SITEURL are defined in wp-config.php, update those constants too — they override the database values.
